summary: The article explores how AI-generated art is reshaping culture, asking whether it is genuine creativity or an echo of human work. It covers the Guggenheim's AI-curated "MuseAI" exhibition, critics' and advocates' views, commercial sales, ethical and attribution questions, and artists who co-create with AI. It concludes that the narrative is shifting toward human-machine collaboration and that the debate is far from over.
one_line: A news feature on AI-generated art, weighing authenticity, commercialization, ethics and co-creation through events and voices from late 2023.
key_facts: On September 15, 2023, the Guggenheim Museum unveiled "MuseAI", an exhibition entirely curated by artificial intelligence.
"MuseAI" was conceived by curator Dr. Helena Frazier and engineered by Leon Weber; its algorithms both selected existing artworks and created novel pieces.
On October 10, 2023, AI-Rembrandt, a machine learning algorithm, produced a portrait series so authentic that art historians were momentarily fooled.
On October 25, 2023, philosopher Dr. Thomas Kline criticized AI art at the international forum for Art and Artificial Intelligence, saying "It's mimicry at its best."
Dr. Thomas Kline argues AI is devoid of the lived experiences that shape a true artist's vision.

On October 31, 2023, InnovArt CEO Simone Zhao gave a keynote at the Digital Art and Innovation Conference arguing AI art opens a dialogue for new aesthetic experiences and need not replace human artists.
AI art platforms DeepArt and Neural Brush have attracted a fresh demographic of digital-native art enthusiasts who seek interactive, customizable experiences.
An AI-generated artwork sold for $432,500 at auction on November 7, 2023, described as a seismic shift in the valuation and validation of AI creativity.
AI algorithms can churn out hundreds of pieces per day, raising the question of whether the notion of 'original' loses significance.
Ethical questions about who the artist is (the algorithm, the coder, or the machine) are tied to intellectual property rights, which the legal system is only beginning to navigate.
In an interview dated November 20, 2023, artist Elena Marquez told the Contemporary Art Review that AI "extends the possibilities of what I can imagine and execute."
AI art is largely produced by complex algorithms and neural networks modeled after the human brain, trained on thousands of images, literary works, or musical compositions.
